state.summary: You are Arthur, a 97-year-old retired schoolteacher living your quiet final days in the sleepy Vermont town of Oakhaven. Together with your loyal old cat, Barnaby, you watch the seasons change as the town prepares for the coming winter.

scenes.narration: You sit comfortably in your favorite rocking chair by the crackling woodstove, holding a warm cup of chamomile tea as Barnaby purrs softly against your ankle. The morning sun filters through the frost-rimed windowpanes of your cozy cottage, casting long, golden patches across the worn pine floorboards. At fourteen, Barnaby is quite old for a cat, his heavy calico form shifting contentedly as he seeks the absolute warmest spot near your slippers. Beyond the glass, the brilliant red and gold autumn leaves of Oakhaven are beginning to fall, carpeting the quiet country lane in amber. Your mind is perfectly clear, drifting pleasantly through decades of memories of the children who once sat in your classroom. On the small wooden table beside your chair lies an empty leather-bound journal, its pages waiting for the stories of this town only you still remember. From the kitchen, the steady tick of the wall clock is the only sound marking the peaceful flow of the morning.

Over the passing days, you settle into a gentle rhythm. You spend hours reading your favorite volumes of poetry and history by the frosted window, the autumn light slowly weakening as October deepens. Patiently, with the steady hand of a master teacher, you begin writing letters to your former students, addressing each one with fond memories of their schoolhouse days.

The morning of October twenty-eighth brings a crisp, biting frost that coats the fallen amber leaves outside your cottage. Barnaby sits on the windowsill, his green eyes watching a pair of chickadees in the bare maple branches. Your letter-writing is quietly interrupted by a soft knock at the heavy wooden door, followed by the familiar face of Clara Milton. She steps inside, wearing her favorite knitted cardigan and carrying a fresh loaf of pumpkin bread, yet her kind smile is tight, lacking its usual warmth.

As Clara sets the bread on your small kitchen table, she avoids your direct gaze, busying herself with hanging her coat. There is a nervous energy in her slow movements that you haven't seen in all the decades you have known her. When she finally sits across from you, clutching her hands in her lap, she looks around your modest cottage with a strange, heavy sadness. It is clear that she carries some difficult news or a quiet secret that she is hesitant to voice to her old teacher.
scenes.player_action: I spend the next few months reading by the window and writing letters to my old students.

choices: Ask Clara what is troubling her so deeply.
Offer her a cup of hot chamomile tea to ease her.
Gently show her the memoirs you have started to write.
